openings.text: Mina set the invitation stack beside the red roof post. “The first moonberry invitation goes out before the rooftop bell!” she cried. Pip puffed a hopeful little smoke-ring, while Jun watched from a chimney with one bright, thoughtful eye.

Mina placed the invitations by the roof post and promised, “Neighbors first, berry feast second!” Pip wiggled his wings, eager to help. Above them, Jun tilted his head toward the quietest corner of the garden, where a pigeon-sized party might be just right.

Mina set the neat invitation stack beside the red post. Pip bounced on his toes. “I can carry, fly, or make it fancy!” he announced. The rooftop bell was still quiet, but the moonberry party was already tugging everyone in three different directions.

variants.text: Mina slid the stack beside the post and tied her promise to it like an invisible bow. “Before the bell,” she said. Pip nodded so hard that a tiny smoke puff escaped his nose.
Mina examined the red post. She discovered that its open hook was marked “safe,” ready for a ribboned invitation. “Aha!” she said, tapping the number with one finger.
Mina peered at the crowded hooks and discovered that only the hook marked “bird-high” was open. Jun gave a pleased coo from above.
Mina inspected the post and discovered a crowded row of hooks, with one open hook tucked between two old sun hats. “There you are,” she whispered.
Mina lifted the top card and discovered delicate paper, soft as a moth wing. She quickly lowered it. “This stack needs gentle feet, not grabby dragon claws.”
Mina fanned the stack and discovered sturdy cards, cheerful and firm. “These can survive a Pip-sized adventure,” she said, though she still reached for a ribbon.
Mina inspected the post and discovered a crowded row of hooks, with hardly any room between two old sun hats. “There you are,” she whispered, choosing a snug place among them.
Mina looked up. “Jun, where should the bird guests gather?” Jun fluttered to the quiet corner and tapped the tiles twice. Mina smiled. “A quiet corner it is.”
Mina told Pip about Jun’s quiet corner, and Pip’s round eyes grew rounder still.
With the post’s open hook in mind, Mina chose its little numbered perch.
With the post’s crowded hooks in mind, Mina chose a snug perch among them for the ribboned invitations.
Mina fastened the paper sail to the sturdy stack. It trembled like a tiny kite. Pip leaned close. “That is either excellent engineering,” he said, “or a very polite napkin.”
Mina handed the invitation stack to Pip, who held it as carefully as a sleepy soap bubble.
Mina passed the berry basket to Jun for the quiet corner, and he tested its handle with one approving peck.
Pip grabbed the stack before Mina could finish saying “gently.” His wings beat once, the cards flapped, and Mina’s eyebrows flew higher than the roof chimney.
“Freeze your toes!” Mina cried. She took back the delicate cards, but one corner had bent into a little paper wave. Pip tucked his claws beneath his chin. “I was trying to be helpful.”

Pip studied the quiet-corner plan, then brightened. “I can decorate one invitation for Jun and fly another for the neighbors!” He offered the paper sail, not his claws. Mina blinked, then began tying the ribbon.
Jun pointed from Mina to Pip, then to the quiet corner. His request was clear at last: one invitation for the bird guests, tucked away from the loudest party whoops.
Mina listened to Pip’s plan and nodded. “One card for Jun’s quiet corner, one for the moonberry crowd.” Pip grinned, and the ribbon between them looked suddenly like a tiny bridge.
Pip agreed to share the adventure, folding his wings around the plan instead of around the whole stack.
Mina carried the ribboned invitations to the chosen hook and posted them neatly. The cards settled against the red post, ready to call the neighbors to moonberries and dancing.
Pip gave the paper sail one brave puff. Up it went, carrying an invitation to the high hook. It landed with a soft papery plop, and Pip beamed as though he had personally taught the sky a new trick.
Jun swooped ahead, marking the quiet route with three silver wingbeats.
Jun guided them to the quiet corner, where the shared invitations arrived beside the berry basket. One card wore a dragon-drawn star; another rested under Jun’s careful wing.
Mina and Pip carried the softened stack together. The cards arrived with curled corners and berry-smudged stars, and every neighbor received one. Pip’s claws stayed under the ribbon this time.
Mina squeezed Pip’s shoulder. “Thank you, my wonderfully wobbly helper.” Pip’s smoke puff came out shaped like a heart.

endings.text: The invitation rested on the high hook, its ribbon fluttering like a tiny flag. Pip beamed below it, wings tucked tight, while the first neighbor spotted the card and waved toward the moonberry garden.

The softened invitations reached the neighbors with curled corners and berry-smudged stars. Mina and Pip stood shoulder to shoulder beneath the roof post, watching each card disappear into a happy pair of hands.

Jun guided a bird-sized invitation into the quiet corner while Pip delivered the party card. Around the berry basket gathered three kinds of footsteps: Mina’s, Pip’s dragon-toes, and Jun’s quick little wingbeats.
The moonberry invitation rested on its chosen hook, bright against the red post. Mina rang the rooftop bell, and somewhere beyond the chimney, a neighbor answered with an excited whoop.

The invitation rested on the high hook, its ribbon fluttering like a tiny flag. Pip’s paper sail had carried it safely, Mina rang the rooftop bell, and a neighbor waved from beyond the chimney. Pip sneezed a silver star.
